nodes.rationale: Running the validator (rather than reading it) narrowed the finding from four states to one: only the ABSENT state slips through, and absence is the default. The fix asserts the absent state, because testing only the value "false" would stay green on top of the original defect.

nodes.label: 22,328 Lines of .astro Never Type-checked
nodes.rationale: tsc cannot parse .astro and skips it silently despite tsconfig include. The withTenant vs withTenantOrThrow class of defect would compile and render a broken page with no red gate. Checked and clean today — what is missing is whatever KEEPS it that way: a truth that holds without a checker is a truth waiting to be changed.

nodes.label: skills:check Exemption and Line-wrap Holes
nodes.rationale: Three holes: an all-or-nothing per-skill exemption, a path extractor blind to paths wrapped across lines by Prettier, and no way to distinguish 'this path exists' from 'this path does NOT exist and that is the point'. The third explains the first: when the only way to write the truth is to exempt the whole skill, people exempt the whole skill.

nodes.label: Accepted ADRs Without a Line of Code
nodes.rationale: Accepted reads as 'present in the code' and nobody checks it; ADR-0020 was Accepted while its artifacts had already been revoked by another ADR that did not mark it Superseded. What is missing is not a gate but VOCABULARY — the status packs 'decided, not built yet' and 'decided, running' into one word.
nodes.norm_label: accepted adrs without a line of code

nodes.label: Compression Is Inherited From Cloudflare
nodes.rationale: The original 'no compression anywhere' finding was wrong on the part that matters: both deployed environments return content-encoding: gzip from Cloudflare, and that topology was already documented — read from the first 180 lines of a 330-line file. Twice in one round, reading part of a source produced a confident and mistaken finding. What remains is an unrecorded dependency on an outer layer, not a performance defect; a second compressor would be two places deciding the same thing.

nodes.label: Purge Reaches Varnish, Not the Serving Tier
nodes.rationale: Publishing invalidates the tier that does not serve and leaves the tier that does serve stale. A lag, not a leak, because s-maxage bounds it to five minutes — but no test can see it, since the acceptance table measures X-Cache from Varnish, the tier that is not answering.
nodes.norm_label: purge reaches varnish, not the serving tier

nodes.label: AWCMS Repository Inventory (generated)
nodes.rationale: A GENERATED block between markers — the tables must never be hand-edited, and the generated figures (not hand greps) are the numbers other documents must cite.

nodes.label: Tables & Row-Level Security Inventory
nodes.rationale: Each awcms_* table is listed with the migration that created it and its RLS/FORCE state, plus a count of RLS-free global-by-design tables.

nodes.label: Resilience & DR Verification (dr-drill)
nodes.rationale: Documented recovery behaviour is only evidence once exercised under a controlled failure; the individual mechanisms have their own tests but nothing tied them into one DR run with a single verdict and RTO/RPO evidence. In this repo the tool is a TARGET specification ported from the base, not running code.

nodes.label: authorizeDrDrill Safety Interlock
nodes.rationale: Stricter than production preflight's authorizeApply in two ways: APP_ENV=production has NO override flag at all (a failure-injection tool has no legitimate use against production), and the database host is default-DENY — an unrecognized hostname is refused, not assumed safe. Widening the allowlist is a reviewed code change, never a runtime flag.

nodes.label: Scenario Catalog with Disclosure
nodes.rationale: Every scenario carries an explicit implemented / simulated / cross-verified disclosure so no scenario claims to do more than it does — e.g. postgres-disconnect is simulated at the CLIENT level and proxies app recovery time, not Postgres restart time.

nodes.label: backup-restore-drill scenario
nodes.rationale: full tier only: real backup, real restore, real RLS/schema verification against a disposable database with drill-only keys; skipped rather than failed when no version-matched pg_dump exists.

nodes.label: worker-interruption scenario
nodes.rationale: Real process, real SIGTERM, real advisory lock, then a second run with the same job name to prove the lock was not left stuck — the dangerous failure mode being two runs of the same job genuinely overlapping (a payroll or posting job double-executing).

nodes.label: provider-outage-email scenario
nodes.rationale: The concrete retry/idempotency proof: exactly 2 provider calls and 2 delivery attempts across a fail-then-recover cycle. R2/object sync is cross-verified rather than re-implemented because it shares the identical outbox + circuit-breaker shape.

nodes.label: Tri-state overall verdict (pass/fail/incomplete)
nodes.rationale: incomplete exists so a reader can never mistake a SKIPPED check for a verified pass; the CLI exits non-zero unless overall is pass.

nodes.label: History of the AWCMS Repo
nodes.rationale: Moved out of README because the README must answer 'what is this, now' and history piling up at the front buries that answer. Not a single claim here binds the state of the repo today.

nodes.label: Off-Supabase Migration (ADR-013…023)
nodes.rationale: mcp, public and admin were each moved to Bun; once Supabase was unused the legacy files were removed — not to retire the repo but to clear the ground for a rebuild on a new standard foundation with a broader business scope.

nodes.label: Technology Base Adopted From awcms-mini
nodes.rationale: Bun-only runtime (ADR-0002), Astro SSR as a single modular-monolith shell, PostgreSQL with mandatory RLS (ADR-0003), modular monolith microservice-ready (ADR-0001), hybrid online-first with an HMAC-signed sync outbox (ADR-0006), validated OpenAPI/AsyncAPI contracts.

nodes.label: Performance and Security Standards Map
nodes.rationale: Adds no new rule — it is the one place stating which standards are followed, which edition, and which controls are NOT met. Unlike the assessment snapshot this document is LIVING and must be updated whenever a control lands or is revoked; a row that cannot be proven is written 'not yet measured', not 'met'.

nodes.label: OWASP Edition Pin (family-level decision)
nodes.rationale: The 2021/4.0.3 pin is INHERITED from a skill, not a decision anyone took. Two family repos on different editions produce two matrices that cannot be added together and readers will misread the numbering difference as a control gap — so raising it is ADR work, and the neighbouring repo follows rather than leads.

nodes.label: Response Security Headers Matrix
nodes.rationale: No 'unsafe-inline' anywhere: the single inline admin theme-init script is allowed by SHA-256 hash — one exact byte sequence, not a class — and a test goes red when body and hash drift, because a hash mismatch fails SILENTLY (script blocked, no error, no log).

nodes.label: Gap Ledger C1–C17
nodes.rationale: Ordered by consequence and each row names the checker that must land with it, because a rule without its checker is a rule that will be broken — including rules that come from external standards. CLOSED rows stay in the table: deleted, they are re-proposed six months later and their checker gets loosened by someone who does not know why it exists.

nodes.label: Recorded Intentional Divergences (family manifest)
nodes.rationale: Five entries with reason/owner/reviewDate 2027-02-04 (HSTS includeSubDomains, .astro not type-checked, the OWASP edition, COOP/CORP isolation, the admin-user surface) — both sides of each difference are correct for their own surface, and recording it prevents one repo's table stating a false fact about the other.

nodes.label: Four Performance Gates
nodes.rationale: db:fk-index:check (pure, always runs), build:asset-budget:check (chained inside build so it runs in CI and release), DB-gated query budgets, and the env-gated CWV lab. 'CI green' is now a far stronger performance guarantee, but field p75 remains absent until the RUM decision is taken.

nodes.label: Controls Deliberately Not Adopted
nodes.rationale: Written down so a rejected control is not re-proposed as a new finding: EDGE_CACHE_MODE on by default (a shared cache before a multi-tenant app is a leak machine), rate limiting that fails CLOSED (a Redis outage would become an attacker-triggerable total login denial), raw per-visit CWV rows (inverts the visitor_analytics privacy posture), gating docs/awcms/ like skills, and raising coverage for the percentage.

nodes.label: Cross-repo Relationship With awcms-astro
nodes.rationale: That repo consumes this one and serves no API, so most controls here have no counterpart there — which does not make them irrelevant: decisions here change what is correct there. Compression is an OWNERSHIP difference, not a quality one; .astro is statically analysed in neither repo and both now say so themselves.

nodes.label: Cloudflare Turnstile Bot Protection
nodes.rationale: A layer ON TOP of rate limiting, lockout, audit and the generic auth error, never a replacement. No migration at all — purely configuration/env, and the secret never touches the DB.

nodes.label: isTurnstileRequired activation gate
nodes.rationale: ONE function gates the widget, the CSP origin and the enforcement, so drift is impossible (e.g. the CSP opened while the widget is not rendered). Requires the full-online profile AND the feature flag, so every LAN/offline deployment renders the login page byte-identical to before with zero outbound calls.

nodes.label: Turnstile Threat Model
nodes.rationale: Enforcement runs BEFORE the identity lookup so a failure is never an account-enumeration oracle; the circuit breaker trips only on TRANSPORT failures so garbage tokens cannot lock out every tenant; hostname and action echoes are validated (mutation-proven); the verify URL comes only from configuration, never request input.

nodes.label: Fail-closed Outage SOP
nodes.rationale: A Cloudflare failure rejects login for the outage's duration — deliberate, not a bug. Mitigations in order: wait for the breaker to retry, or temporarily downgrade the profile and record the decision. Never disable rate limit or lockout as compensation — that removes exactly the layer that still works.

nodes.label: Turnstile Configuration Reference
nodes.rationale: Cross-rules distinguish MISCONFIGURED from intentionally disabled; credentials may be staged before the profile gate is opened; readiness checks print only the missing variable's NAME, never a secret value.

nodes.label: Privacy-first Opt-in Defaults
nodes.rationale: OFF with no configuration at all; raw IP, raw user-agent and geolocation stay independently off even once enabled, geolocation comes from a header already on the request (never an external call), and raw_detail.read is a separate permission from dashboard.read. A software setting is NOT a legal basis — the operator must establish one under UU PDP before enabling collection.

nodes.label: Anonymous awcms_visitor_key Cookie
nodes.rationale: Cut from ~2 years to a configurable 30 days; rotation is the cookie TTL itself (no server bookkeeping), and the cookie is ACTIVELY revoked before the path/area gate whenever the module is not enabled, so a browser carrying an old identifier does not keep it merely because nothing refreshes it.

nodes.label: Tiered Retention (raw < event < rollup)
nodes.rationale: Shorter retention for more sensitive data: raw detail 30 days is cleared IN PLACE (the aggregate browser/device fields stay useful), events and sessions 90 days hard-deleted, rollups 730 days. The ordering is an invariant enforced by readiness checks — critical for genuinely active raw IP, warning otherwise, since an operator may consciously accept an inverted ordering.

nodes.label: analytics:rollup job
nodes.rationale: Idempotent by construction — each run recomputes full totals and UPSERTs, never adding to the old value; an area with no events gets no row rather than a zero row; it never copies raw ip_address or identifier snapshots into the aggregate table.

nodes.label: analytics:purge job
nodes.rationale: Calls the SAME purge function as the on-demand endpoint rather than re-deriving its own rules, and adds no second batching layer for the same reason. Sessions are deleted only when no events still reference them (NOT EXISTS). Only tenants that actually had rows removed get an audit event, whose attributes are four summary numbers — never raw data.

nodes.label: Six security:readiness Cross-field Checks
nodes.rationale: Cross-field SECURITY JUDGEMENT lives in security-readiness (which has CheckSeverity and out-of-scope honesty), while single-variable SHAPE validation stays in validate-env — duplicating CheckSeverity into validate-env, which never had it, is what this split avoids. Geo active without Cloudflare trust is critical precisely so the operator does not believe a feature is active while it is silently empty.

nodes.label: UU PDP / ISO / ASVS Compliance Mapping
nodes.rationale: Maps controls ALREADY implemented (not aspirations) to UU PDP articles, PP PSTE, ISO 27001/27002/27005/27701, ASVS and the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet. Risk treatment is avoidance-by-default rather than mitigation-after-the-fact; residual risks (no local GeoIP, an empty hash salt only warning) are accepted explicitly rather than ignored. Telemetry collection is deliberately fail-OPEN, in contrast to ABAC/RLS which are always fail-closed.
nodes.norm_label: uu pdp / iso / asvs compliance mapping

nodes.label: Minimal Domain Module Example (expense-category)
nodes.rationale: A template, not a module that exists: the most minimal ERP domain that still makes sense (one master-data entity, no transaction/approval flow). Copy the pattern and change the domain, entities, permissions and fields — do not copy expense-category into production.

nodes.label: Initial ModuleDescriptor Template
nodes.rationale: A new module always starts at version 0.1.0 / status experimental and moves to active only after integration tests and the security checklist; it depends on identity_access because it uses that module's evaluateAccess/resolveTenantContext rather than rewriting its own RBAC/ABAC.

nodes.label: Migration + ENABLE/FORCE RLS Template
nodes.rationale: ENABLE and FORCE must be in the SAME migration that creates the table — RLS without FORCE does not apply to the owner/migration role. Indexes are prefixed with (tenant_id, …), and a new table still needs its own explicit GRANT to the least-privilege application role.

nodes.label: Thin Route Pattern
nodes.rationale: auth → tenant context → ABAC guard + decision log → validation → idempotency when high-risk → service inside the transaction → response helper. Astro routes stay in src/pages/api/v1/…, never inside the module folder; application functions take the tx and never open their own connection; pure validation lives in domain/ with no DB import.

nodes.label: Production-ready Security Checklist
nodes.rationale: Includes a security TEST that RLS genuinely is FORCE (a cross-tenant query must return 0 rows, not merely 'look right' on the happy path) and that ABAC default-deny holds when a permission is not seeded — there is no implicit grant.

nodes.label: Per-module OpenAPI Fragment Pattern
nodes.rationale: The published contract stays a single bundled file; only the SOURCE is split one fragment per module. api:spec:check fails on a stale bundle, a duplicated operationId, a mismatched path parameter, a non-ApiError error response, or implicit security metadata.

nodes.label: Jualanku.info Implementation Blueprint
nodes.rationale: A PLAN, not a description of code: no jualanku module, table, migration, route or permission exists. It translates the PT TIM SIX validation document v1.0 into an executable design AFTER correcting it against the real code — if the document differs from the code, the code is right.

nodes.label: P0 Prerequisites Before the First Line of Code
nodes.rationale: The order is binding because each item produces an artifact the next one uses: ADRs, module-inventory reconciliation, the cross-origin session contract, the merchant/business-scope model with a negative-authorization matrix that must be RED before any code exists, then five frozen descriptors.
nodes.norm_label: p0 prerequisites before the first line of code

nodes.label: Rules That Bind the Implementation
nodes.rationale: Taken from contracts that already apply, not new rules: modules live directly in src/modules (no derived repo), FORCE RLS on every tenant table written only by its owning module, defineTenantRoute plus a default-deny guard whose resourceAttributes come from the real row, a new permission means a new seed migration (older tenants stay 403 until backfilled), high-risk actions carry idempotency+audit+decision log with declared sodRules, and one OpenAPI fragment per module.

nodes.label: Layer Split (experience vs platform)
nodes.rationale: Each layer is defined as much by what it is NOT responsible for: the experience layer owns no business rules or database access, the platform owns no public markup, and the edge owns no authorization — a cache is not access control.

nodes.label: Deployment Topology (public host vs admin host)
nodes.rationale: awcms is not published as a general-purpose API; the admin host is separate from the public host because a single origin serving merchant and admin pages turns every CSP, cookie or cache mistake into a cross-audience mistake.
nodes.norm_label: deployment topology (public host vs admin host)

nodes.label: Rendering Matrix per Surface
nodes.rationale: Static-by-default with on-demand routes: modern Astro has only static or server output, and mixed capability comes from per-route prerender=false once an adapter is installed, not from a hybrid output value that no longer exists. Portal and admin surfaces are private, no-store.

nodes.label: Why the BFF Is Mandatory
nodes.rationale: Six reasons, each closing one concrete failure: the tenant must not be decided by the browser, no tokens in browser storage, CSRF/Origin/cache policy applied in one place, the envelope projected into a view model, per-audience rate limits, and a small attack surface with one trusted client. Hard boundary: the BFF must not decide anything with business consequences — a check that exists only there does not exist, since a direct internal call bypasses it.

nodes.label: Reuse of Existing Website Modules
nodes.rationale: Jualanku rebuilds nothing that exists: blog_content, seo_distribution, site_search, media_library, theming, tenant_domain, visitor_analytics, comments, data_lifecycle, email, workflow_approval + SoD, and form_drafts are consumed through their existing seams. The only genuinely new things are the five domain modules.

nodes.label: Tenant, Merchant, Role and Authorization
nodes.rationale: The security backbone of the porting, built on one sentence: RLS separates TENANTS, not merchants. One operator tenant holds merchants as domain entities, so cross-merchant directory and moderation stay ordinary queries — and merchant isolation is not free, it has to be built.

nodes.label: Six Layers of Isolation
nodes.rationale: Tenant, merchant, role, workflow, data field and surface — each row names what its FAILURE looks like, so a control is judged by the leak it prevents rather than by its presence.

nodes.label: Merchant as a Business Scope
nodes.rationale: Membership is a scope grant with effective dating, so revocation and expiry take effect from server now with no cleanup job. TWO safety belts, not one: ABAC as the policy layer and an ownership predicate in every query, so a wrongly written policy still returns no rows belonging to someone else. The base hierarchy resolver returns resolved:false for every type, which default-denies high-risk actions — safe but non-functional until a module provides the hierarchy.

nodes.label: Persona / Role Catalogue
nodes.rationale: Ordinary tenant roles seeded by migration; finance maker and checker are separate roles, and merchant/affiliate/onboarding roles never receive any internal module permission or admin navigation entry.

nodes.label: Permissions Must Use the Existing AccessAction Union
nodes.rationale: There is no submit, payout or verify action: an action outside the union produces a permission that is never seeded and a silent deny against even the tenant owner, green in CI because nothing tests it. Submission maps to create, approval to approve (its SoD counterpart), policy/commission changes to configure rather than update.
nodes.norm_label: permissions must use the existing accessaction union

nodes.label: Mandatory ABAC Rules
nodes.rationale: Written only with attributes already in the allow-list. An approver may not approve what they created — expressed as an ABAC deny AND sodRules, both, because one alone is a single point of failure. Resource attributes always come from the real row: a merchantId in the body is validated input, never a trusted claim.

nodes.label: Negative-authorization Test Matrix
nodes.rationale: Thirteen scenarios written BEFORE the implementation and required to be red first — green from the start means the test tests nothing. Cross-merchant reads answer 404 anti-oracle rather than a 403 that confirms existence, and the RLS case must be run as awcms_app because on a PaaS whose default user is a superuser FORCE RLS is silently inert while migrations stay green.

nodes.label: Five Bounded Contexts and the Data Model
nodes.rationale: Five contexts, not seven: module boundaries follow invariants, data ownership and change patterns rather than menu structure, and further splitting happens only once coupling has been measured.
nodes.norm_label: five bounded contexts and the data model

nodes.label: jualanku_directory module
nodes.rationale: Owns merchants, membership, taxonomy, locations, business pages and publication, and PROVIDES the merchant scope hierarchy capability — without it high-risk merchant actions deny because the resolver returns resolved:false. The public projection is published rows not held by moderation; drafts are never queried from the public namespace.

nodes.label: jualanku_catalog_growth module
nodes.rationale: Owns offerings, promotions, leads and interactions. The interactions table is the ONLY one accepting writes from a public surface, so it is privacy-minimized (no fingerprint), idempotent, separately rate-limited, and never a source of authorization. Lead contact PII is hashed and masked, never raw in a list.

nodes.label: jualanku_affiliate module
nodes.rationale: Owns affiliates, links, clicks, conversions and fraud flags. Link codes must not be sequentially guessable, conversion status transitions are append-only in an event table, and self-referral is a rule rather than an optional heuristic.

nodes.label: jualanku_commercial module
nodes.rationale: Owns plans, entitlements, subscriptions, invoices, the commission ledger and payout requests. The ledger is append-only — a correction is a new entry, never an UPDATE — and the available balance is computed from the ledger, not from a conversion total. An external provider is never called inside a database transaction.

nodes.label: jualanku_trust_operations module
nodes.rationale: Owns verification cases, moderation, complaints, appeals and onboarding assignments. A merchant cannot approve itself, an appeal is decided by someone other than the original decider, moderation holds publication without deleting data, and a complaint channel is mandatory before go-live under Law 8/1999.

nodes.label: Composite FK and Table Conventions
nodes.rationale: FKs between tenant-scoped tables are composite (tenant_id, id) because a plain FK bypasses RLS and becomes a cross-tenant leak path; the target needs UNIQUE (tenant_id, id). Money is numeric, time is timestamptz, and the ownership column is named merchant_id in EVERY context so ownership predicates can be reviewed with a single grep. Migration numbers are never written into the document — an applied migration is immutable.

nodes.label: One Table, One Writing Module
nodes.rationale: Other modules read through an application service, capability port, read model or domain event — never a direct join into someone else's table, not even from a job. commercial and affiliate must not depend on catalog_growth; their relationship goes through events. A capability changes the capability graph, not the dependency DAG.

nodes.label: Personal Data Classes and Retention
nodes.rationale: Identifiers stored normalized+hashed and displayed masked per purpose; verification evidence never gets a public URL; clicks and interactions get short retention; the ledger and invoices get long retention with legal hold. Subject requests use the existing data_lifecycle mechanism and retained data is explained to the requester.

nodes.label: Three Namespaces, One Implementation of the Rules
nodes.rationale: public, portal (called only by the BFF) and admin all call the SAME application service; only authentication, authorization, accepted input and response projection differ. A business rule written twice is a defect regardless of whether the two copies currently agree.
nodes.norm_label: three namespaces, one implementation of the rules

nodes.label: Binding Minimum API Controls
nodes.rationale: Per-module OpenAPI fragment, AsyncAPI with PII classification and dead-lettering, a standard envelope, stable error codes, keyset pagination whose cursor carries created_at as full-precision TEXT (Postgres microseconds vs JS milliseconds skips rows), idempotency on payout/invoice/publish/import/interaction ingest, ETag optimistic locking, audit with correlation ID, per-audience rate limits, and security headers via middleware.

nodes.label: Jualanku Domain Events
nodes.rationale: Events are the only automatic path between contexts — no context writes another context's tables. merchant.published drives search/SEO/purge, conversion.recorded drives commission accrual, payout.decided drives email and reporting.

nodes.label: Deliberately Not Built in the Initial Phase
nodes.rationale: No marketplace checkout/escrow/wallet/logistics, no second search endpoint (site_search exists), no second identity system, no public endpoint that accepts merchantId as the determinant of ownership, and no outbound webhooks before there is a contract, retry policy and data classification.
nodes.norm_label: deliberately not built in the initial phase

nodes.label: Cross-origin Session Contract and the BFF
nodes.rationale: What is missing is not cookie support — login already sets httpOnly cookies and the guard accepts header OR cookie — but a session contract for a DIFFERENT ORIGIN: the awcms cookie belongs to the awcms origin and a browser on the public domain will never send it, and must not.
nodes.norm_label: cross-origin session contract and the bff

nodes.label: GET /api/v1/auth/session introspection
nodes.rationale: Owned by identity_access and called by the BFF, never the browser. Returns safe claims only — never the token, its hash, password status, MFA secrets or raw contact details — and is fail-closed and anti-oracle: invalid, expired and revoked all produce the identical 401 shape. The rejected alternative was letting the public browser call the API with cross-site cookies, which moves tenant selection, CSRF and CORS onto the client.

nodes.label: BFF Obligations
nodes.rationale: The awcms token stays server-side, never in JS; CSRF needs an Origin/Referer check PLUS a token, not one of them; the tenant is set from the host mapping and a client tenant header is ignored entirely; logout calls awcms FIRST and only then deletes the portal cookie, because the reverse order leaves a live session; revocation authority stays in awcms and the BFF keeps no session list of its own.

nodes.label: Condensed BFF Threat Model
nodes.rationale: Covers token theft via XSS, CSRF, fixation, the confused deputy (the BFF exposes an explicit upstream route list, never a generic passthrough), tenant tampering, private data reaching a cache or sitemap, enumeration, and mutation replay. Tests must assert field by field, so a newly leaked claim turns a test red.

nodes.label: Porting the UI/UX and Design System
nodes.rationale: Porting means translating user goals, hierarchy, patterns, copy, states and behaviour — not copying WordPress DOM, CSS classes, widgets, shortcodes, plugins or the data model. Not a single line of WordPress markup comes across.
nodes.norm_label: porting the ui/ux and design system

nodes.label: Elementor Migration Disposition Matrix
nodes.rationale: PORT / REDESIGN / DYNAMIC / REMOVE / DEFER per route and section, each row naming its data owner and accessibility notes; placeholders, demo PII and hard-coded links never reach production, and benefit claims need an evidence owner and legal sign-off.

nodes.label: Shared Design Tokens via theming
nodes.rationale: No new token system: existing AWCMS tokens get their values through the theming module per tenant. Solid fills use the -strong variant because the plain token fails AA in some combinations, and status is never distinguished by colour alone.

nodes.label: Jualanku Internal Admin Screens
nodes.rationale: SSR under /admin/jualanku/** registered through the module's navigation descriptor — the menu is built from the registry, so an entry pointing at a 404 turns the navigation test red. Scripts are imported and bundled (no inline scripts, CSP). Merchants and affiliates have no route, navigation entry, role or session audience here.

nodes.label: WCAG 2.2 AA Accessibility Baseline
nodes.rationale: Raised from the template's 2.1 AA (adopted as ISO/IEC 40500:2025): keyboard operability with visible focus, 44 CSS px touch targets, server-side validation because client validation is not a control, prefers-reduced-motion honoured by turning decoration OFF rather than speeding it up, and automated plus manual testing on critical flows.

nodes.label: Roadmap, Quality Gates, KPIs and Compliance
nodes.rationale: Phases P0–P6 each with exit criteria, broken into atomic units of work: one bounded context or surface slice per PR carrying migration, seed, OpenAPI fragment, tests, docs and changeset.
nodes.norm_label: roadmap, quality gates, kpis and compliance

nodes.label: Blocking Quality Gates
nodes.rationale: The existing full check chain plus security:readiness and family:conformance:check, with RLS isolation verified as awcms_app rather than a superuser; Jualanku adds zero-tolerance counts (no tokens in browser storage, no private routes in sitemap or public cache, no demo PII) and an ASVS 5.0 L2 profile for portal and admin.

nodes.label: GO / PIVOT / PAUSE / STOP Criteria
nodes.rationale: PAUSE is triggered by unproven cross-merchant authorization, a browser-manipulable tenant context, private responses reaching a cache, or payouts without a ledger and maker-checker. STOP covers checkout/escrow/wallet before PMF, microservices or complex AI without a quantified need, and any feature lacking an owner, contract, lifecycle, permissions, audit, KPIs and exit criteria.

nodes.label: Standards Baseline (ISO/OWASP/WCAG)
nodes.rationale: ISO/IEC 27034-1 + ASVS 5.0, API Security Top 10 2023, 27001:2022 with 27002 guidance, 27005, 27701:2025, 27018:2025, a 27017 transition watch, 25010:2023, 29148 and 42001 only if AI becomes material. ISO/IEC 15408 is used only as a concept on session/authorization components — there is NO EAL or certification claim of any kind.

nodes.label: Indonesian Regulatory Mapping
nodes.rationale: UU PDP 27/2022, UU 1/2024 (ITE), PP 71/2019 PSTE, Permenkominfo 5/2020 jo 10/2021, PP 80/2019 PMSE, Permendag 19/2026 and UU 8/1999. The PMSE classification must not be assumed from branding — Finance/Risk/Compliance writes a legal memo from the REAL production features.

nodes.label: Corrections to Validation Document v1.0
nodes.rationale: The validation document partly reasons from repo DOCUMENTATION, and documentation can be stale; every line was rechecked against the code. What is confirmed is not repeated, what differs is recorded with its evidence — including that news_portal was MERGED into blog_content rather than never built.

nodes.label: The ABAC Attribute Allow-list Is Closed
nodes.rationale: subject.merchantIds / resource.merchantId cannot be implemented as written: an attribute outside the list is invalid at authoring time and denied at evaluation time, and adding a per-product pair would turn a bounded allow-list into a list that grows on request — losing the very property that makes it valuable. A merchant is modelled as a business scope instead.
nodes.norm_label: the abac attribute allow-list is closed

nodes.label: RLS Can Silently Fail to Separate Tenants
nodes.rationale: FORCE RLS does not apply to a superuser role, and several PaaS providers make the default Postgres user a superuser — if the runtime URL points there, tenant isolation is lost entirely while migrations stay green and the health check returns 200. Verification must run as awcms_app and be part of the tests, not an assumption.
nodes.norm_label: rls can silently fail to separate tenants

nodes.label: Static-by-default With On-demand Routes
nodes.rationale: 'Hybrid application' is not the right term for modern Astro: output is only static or server, and mixed capability comes from per-route prerender=false. Also corrected: awcms-astro has since moved to Bun, so the derived 'keep Node/npm' conclusion no longer holds — the whole family is Bun-only.

nodes.label: Definition of Ready (flow step 9)
nodes.rationale: Checked at the START, where the Definition of Done is checked at the end. It asks whether the plan can be carried out and whether its specifications agree — it does not demand a complete design, and estimates are deliberately not part of it.

nodes.label: Does Policy Permit Every Read and Write This Plan Needs?
nodes.rationale: Born from two consecutive waves that planned cross-tenant reads FORCE RLS forbids (an audit row in every reachable tenant; a membership list in a 409 response) — both plausible on paper, both caught only at implementation time after code was written on a false premise. Not 'is there a permission' but does RLS allow it, verified by running the query as awcms_app: zero rows is an answer, not a setup failure. Paired with 'what will PROVE it, and which mutation turns it red'.
nodes.norm_label: does policy permit every read and write this plan needs?

nodes.label: Module Admission Decision Checklist
nodes.rationale: A reviewer checklist that summarises the module admission governance document rather than replacing it. The category is determined by decision tree, not assumed; any proposal involving runtime code upload/install/marketplace/eval from tenant or third-party input is rejected outright absent a superseding ADR.

nodes.label: External Provider Governance
nodes.rationale: Off by default, credentials only from env/secret manager, outbound calls OUTSIDE any DB transaction (claim/call/finalize), SSRF validation of provider hosts even when the URL comes from env, per-provider circuit breaker and timeout, graceful degradation that keeps the core operational flow working, minimised/masked payloads with the PII crossing the trust boundary documented, redacted provider errors, and audit on configuration or credential changes.

nodes.label: Deprecation and Removal Rules
nodes.rationale: Posted/append-only data of a removed module is never deleted silently — finance and audit data often carry a legal retention obligation, so the archive plan is decided before the deprecation window; removed routes and events are a major-bump breaking change reflected in OpenAPI/AsyncAPI.

nodes.label: Module category taxonomy (System / Official Optional / ERP domain / External Integration)
nodes.norm_label: module category taxonomy (system / official optional / erp domain / external integration)

nodes.label: offline-lan-safe vs full-online-only compatibility class
nodes.rationale: A module declared full-online-only must prove the offline-lan profile stays 100% functional while the feature is off, so choosing an online-only capability never silently degrades LAN deployments.

nodes.label: The price of having no staging
nodes.rationale: ADR-0083 accepts that this repo has no staging; the cost is paid on the line recording what appeared in production but not in CI, and collecting it release after release is the only way to know whether the trade is still worth it.
nodes.norm_label: the price of having no staging

nodes.label: A review that always produces an action invents actions
nodes.rationale: "None" is a legitimate outcome for both Surprises and What changed, and must be written down; forcing an action item every release manufactures work rather than recording truth.
nodes.norm_label: a review that always produces an action invents actions

nodes.label: New table requires a dataLifecycle descriptor
nodes.norm_label: new table requires a datalifecycle descriptor

nodes.label: GLOBAL / no-RLS data almost always needs an ADR
nodes.rationale: Tenant-scoped data is covered by RLS plus a chokepoint permission; data placed outside RLS loses that boundary, so the decision must be visible as an ADR naming the compensating control.
nodes.norm_label: global / no-rls data almost always needs an adr

nodes.label: openapi:bundle merge pipeline
nodes.rationale: The root fragment plus every openapi/modules/*.openapi.yaml are merged by scripts/openapi-bundle.ts into one published artifact; sources are edited, never the generated bundle, so a module owns exactly the paths carrying its tag and shared components live in one place.

nodes.label: Self-service subscriptions vs ABAC chokepoint
nodes.rationale: /push/subscriptions accepts no recipient and its subject is the caller, so holding the session for a device IS the authorization to manage it (ADR-0049 §7); diagnostics, cancel and test touch other people's rows or make the deployment emit traffic and therefore go through the ABAC chokepoint.

nodes.label: Office schema and keyset-paginated office list
nodes.norm_label: office schema and keyset-paginated office list

nodes.label: Generated inventory beats a hand-written table
nodes.rationale: The hand-written version listed 12 of 52 scripts as active and called fifteen already-landed tools "not yet ported". Negative claims rot silently and never fail on their own, unlike a positive claim that breaks the moment code changes — so the table is generated from package.json and scripts:inventory:check fails when stale.
nodes.norm_label: generated inventory beats a hand-written table

nodes.label: What the check chain may not require
nodes.rationale: bun run check must be safe on any local checkout without a database, without a server and without PR context; targets needing a migrated DB, a live provider, a PR diff or a version tag sit outside the chain for exactly one of those reasons.
nodes.norm_label: what the check chain may not require

nodes.label: ModuleDescriptor.jobs is the job-schedule source of truth
nodes.norm_label: moduledescriptor.jobs is the job-schedule source of truth

nodes.label: src/lib is technical infrastructure only (ADR-0043)
nodes.rationale: src/lib had grown into a second module system guarded by no gate: four namespaces (seo, theming, comments, search) carried a module's name and held that module's code, and seo_distribution referenced upwards into src/lib/seo through a path the DAG validator cannot see. The cause was structural — the module contract had no home for presentation code — so modules:dag:check now fails on a namespace that collides with a moduleKey or a registered domain alias, with logging as the single recorded exception.

nodes.label: Database role separation behind client.ts
nodes.rationale: awcms_app is not a superuser, not BYPASSRLS and not the table owner, with a fail-closed default GUC app.current_tenant_id of the zero UUID — so without withTenant the result is zero rows, and only under this role does RLS FORCE become a real boundary.

nodes.label: Work-class gate + circuit breaker in front of the pool
nodes.norm_label: work-class gate + circuit breaker in front of the pool

nodes.label: Author-own-draft ABAC ownership override
nodes.rationale: One permission must satisfy two demands at once — an Editor/Admin may edit every post, and an Author may edit their own unpublished draft without it — so evaluateContentUpdateAccess expresses an OR on top of evaluateAccess. It is deliberately NOT added to the cross-module deny-biased evaluator: an ALLOW override based on resource ownership is blog_content business logic, applied only when the sole deny reason is default_deny.

nodes.label: Append-only revision history
nodes.rationale: Restoring a revision writes the old content back through the ordinary update and then appends a new revision recording the restored state, so no existing row is ever UPDATEd or DELETEd and the in-between history stays readable.

nodes.label: Content quality checklist gate on publish/schedule
nodes.norm_label: content quality checklist gate on publish/schedule

nodes.label: Scheduled publishing job
nodes.rationale: Restructured from one set-based UPDATE into SELECT ... FOR UPDATE plus a per-post loop, because without it a tenant could bypass the checklist by scheduling a post before enabling R2-only mode and waiting for it to fall due; FOR UPDATE also keeps two concurrent workers safe for the same tenant.

nodes.label: Public /blog/{tenantCode} routes (ADR-0009)
nodes.rationale: All seven are APIRoutes rather than .astro pages because the repo has no test convention for .astro output; writing them as .astro would make the issue's mandatory end-to-end leakage/SEO/feed tests impossible through the established harness.

nodes.label: Two public visibility predicates (listing vs detail)
nodes.rationale: Listing/search/feed/sitemap use strict visibility='public'; detail allows public OR unlisted, because unlisted only means excluded from listings and must stay reachable by direct link — otherwise the unlisted tier would be indistinguishable from private. Both predicates live in one file so a reinterpretation touches one place, not seven route handlers.
nodes.norm_label: two public visibility predicates (listing vs detail)

nodes.label: Whitelist content-block renderer
nodes.rationale: Every block type emits text only through escapeHtml and unknown blocks are skipped silently; adding a type means a new switch case, never a raw-HTML escape hatch.

nodes.label: The retired /news route family (ADR-0071)
nodes.rationale: The four host-resolved /news routes were ON by default, so their URLs were real, indexed and advertised by this repo's own sitemap and feed; retiring them therefore installs a 301 to /blog/{tenantCode} rather than a 404, and the redirect is not policy-gated because nobody can choose to keep serving deleted routes. The single exception is a tenant with legacyTenantRouteEnabled false, which has no /blog either.

nodes.label: Effective public route settings from two stores
nodes.rationale: rssEnabled/sitemapEnabled are deliberately kept out of the module descriptor defaults: a second independently-writable copy in awcms_module_settings would let an admin switch RSS off in one store while the feed route keeps reading the old value — two disconnected sources of truth, a real correctness bug rather than a style preference. publicBasePath is not adopted because it would advertise URLs no file route serves.
nodes.norm_label: effective public route settings from two stores

nodes.label: Clamped offset pagination on public archives
nodes.rationale: ?page=1e8 became OFFSET 1e9 (a one-request DoS holding a pool connection) and ?page=abc became OFFSET NaN → 500; junk now normalises to page 1 rather than a 400, because an HTML archive route must render the first page instead of an error crawlers would index.
nodes.norm_label: clamped offset pagination on public archives

nodes.label: blog_content AsyncAPI domain events
nodes.rationale: Contract documentation only: there is no pub/sub dispatcher, the real producer is the structured JSON logger, and the log line drops the awcms. prefix from the event type.

nodes.label: commentableResources descriptor contribution
nodes.rationale: comments depends on Core only and never imports a content module; content modules declare commentable tables/columns plus a declarative publicationFilter, discovered through listModules(). It is a descriptor list rather than a capability provides because many content modules will want comments and a second provider would trip capability_provider_conflict.

nodes.label: Escape-then-autolink renderer
nodes.rationale: Bodies are stored as raw plain text, never HTML; at render time every character is escaped first and only then are bare http(s) URLs autolinked with rel=nofollow ugc noopener noreferrer — so there is no sanitizer allow-list to get wrong and no path by which a stored comment reaches a browser as markup.

nodes.label: No oracle: uniform public responses
nodes.rationale: An unresolved resource, a disabled module, an anti-abuse block and an accepted-but-pending comment all return the same body, and author-bound operations answer 404 rather than 403, so the endpoint cannot confirm blocked terms, unpublished content, or another author's comment.

nodes.label: Server-side anti-abuse stack
nodes.rationale: Honeypot, HMAC-signed submit-timing floor, length/link bounds, per-tenant blocked terms, duplicate fingerprint and per-IP rate limits all fail closed — with a timing floor configured a missing measurement counts as too fast, so stripping the token is not a bypass.

nodes.label: Minimized commenter PII
nodes.rationale: Author email is stored only as a sha256 hash plus a masked form, IP and user-agent are tenant-salted hashes, and subscription addresses are AES-256-GCM encrypted under their own key — with no key configured an unresolvable sentinel is stored rather than plaintext.

nodes.label: comments:retention anonymization sweep
nodes.rationale: Aged comments are anonymized in place and never deleted, because the append-only moderation history must keep pointing at a row; the sweep skips any tenant under an active legal hold on comments.comments.

nodes.label: HighVolumeTableDescriptor contract
nodes.rationale: Trusted code-only metadata, never tenant- or request-controlled and never duplicated into a mutable settings table; each module declares its own array and a central aggregator reads listModules().

nodes.label: executionMode: delegated vs generic
nodes.rationale: A delegated table keeps its own existing purge job as the sole mutator and this engine only reads it for dry-run visibility; a generic table opts into the engine's own bounded archive/purge using only declared metadata. The one generic adopter is data_lifecycle's own run-history table — dogfooding is the only way to prove non-delegated execution without reaching into another module's schema (ADR-0013 §6, no shared-table write).

nodes.label: Legal holds override retention
nodes.rationale: A hold is checked before anything else that could report a row purgeable, and descriptor metadata cannot declare it away: legalHold.applicable is guidance only and is deliberately not consulted by the enforcement path, while retentionDaysOverride cannot widen eligibility around a hold. create and release are separate permissions bound by a maker/checker SoD rule, since a role holding create must not implicitly hold release.

nodes.label: LegalHoldGuardPort cross-module enforcement
nodes.rationale: Because the engine never mutates a delegated table, the delegated adopter's own purge function is the real enforcement point; the concrete adapter is wired at each composition root rather than imported from inside logging/visitor_analytics, which would be a forbidden circular import (ADR-0011).

nodes.label: Bounded archive/purge engine
nodes.rationale: Real archive/purge execution is deliberately not exposed over HTTP — it is an unattended maintenance operation, not a user action — and legal holds are re-fetched fresh per batch pass so a hold created mid-backlog takes effect on the very next pass.

nodes.label: Cursor boundary safety margin (1ms)
nodes.rationale: timestamptz has microsecond resolution but a value read back through Bun.SQL as a JS Date only has milliseconds, truncating DOWN; comparing un-padded truncated values permanently excluded the boundary row — one row short every archive cycle — and looped the resume on the same last row.

nodes.label: Provider-neutral archive port
nodes.rationale: Only a local filesystem JSONL/CSV adapter exists, SHA-256 checksummed with one manifest row per artifact; ArchivePort.read never writes back into the source table, so a real restore stays a documented operator procedure that goes through the OWNING module's own code.

nodes.label: Lifecycle registry validation gate
nodes.rationale: Pure, no I/O, wired into bun run check and re-checked by security:readiness as defense in depth so the constraint is visible from the go-live checklist and not only from CI.

nodes.label: appendDomainEvent outbox producer
nodes.rationale: Called inside the producer's own business transaction (ADR-0006 compliant, plain DB writes only), so the event row and its per-consumer delivery rows commit atomically with the source state change and a rolled-back transaction produces no dispatchable event by construction.

nodes.label: Versioned event-type registry
nodes.rationale: appendDomainEvent refuses to persist an event whose (eventType, eventVersion) is not listed, stopping silent drift from the published AsyncAPI contract.

nodes.label: Static consumer registry
nodes.rationale: A plain array of consumer definitions so the full fan-out for any event type is knowable from source alone; fan-out is decided at publish time.

nodes.label: Delivery dispatcher
nodes.rationale: Head-of-line ordering per order_key rather than a global total order, with exponential backoff and dead-letter transitions; pure PostgreSQL/in-process operation with no external egress, so offline/LAN deployments are unaffected.

nodes.label: applyConsumerEffectOnce idempotency marker
nodes.rationale: Guarantees a consumer's side effect runs at most once per (consumer, event) under legitimate redelivery — at-least-once delivery, never exactly-once.

nodes.label: Operator-safe delivery replay
nodes.rationale: Permission-gated, reason-required, Idempotency-Key-guarded, audited, and refuses to replay against an incompatible consumer schema; the admin screen sends a key for replay because each call does new work but none for pause/resume, which are naturally idempotent.

nodes.label: EmailProvider port contract
nodes.rationale: One interface with concrete adapters resolved at a single edge and never imported by name elsewhere — directly analogous to sync-storage's ObjectUploader; retryable in the delivery result distinguishes a transient failure worth retrying from a permanent one.

nodes.label: Dispatcher claim lease read-back
nodes.rationale: Provider calls never happen inside a DB transaction (ADR-0006): rows are claimed in a short transaction with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED reusing next_attempt_at as the lease, sent outside any transaction, then finalized. The lease is read back so a row left sending by a dead worker is re-claimed once it expires — otherwise it is permanent limbo. The accepted trade-off is one possible duplicate send when a crash lands between provider-accepted and finalize.

nodes.label: Log email provider (EMAIL_PROVIDER=log)
nodes.rationale: Writes a structured log line with the recipient masked instead of calling a real provider — different from EMAIL_ENABLED=false, where the dispatcher never claims rows at all.

nodes.label: Template category variable allow-list
nodes.rationale: template_key doubles as the category; unlisted caller variables are silently dropped rather than substituted, an unknown category is rejected at create (fail-closed), and htmlBody is HTML-escaped on top of write-time rejection of script/iframe/event-handler markup.

nodes.label: Announcement targeting and bounds
nodes.rationale: Two-tier ABAC — every request needs notification.create, and unbounded role/tenant targets additionally need announcement.create. Preview returns only a matched count and a synthetic sample, never a recipient list; role/tenant targets are capped at 5000 and enqueued via multi-row unnest INSERTs, with truncation reported rather than silent.

nodes.label: Opaque JSONB payload owned by the creating module
nodes.rationale: What a payload means belongs to whichever module created it; never inspecting it beyond the safety rules is what lets one table serve every multi-step form without this module accumulating domain knowledge it would then have to keep in sync.
nodes.norm_label: opaque jsonb payload owned by the creating module

nodes.label: Secret-shaped keys are rejected, not redacted
nodes.rationale: Any key at any nesting depth matching password/token/secret/credential/api_key/private_key fails the whole write with a 400 naming the path, because a caller that gets a 200 cannot tell a stripped field from a saved one and would believe the secret round-tripped.
nodes.norm_label: secret-shaped keys are rejected, not redacted

nodes.label: Idempotency asymmetry between create and submit
nodes.rationale: A retried create costs one deletable scratch row; a retried submit hands the payload to a domain action twice. Requiring a key everywhere trains callers to generate throwaway ones, weakening the guarantee exactly where it matters. There is likewise no separate submit permission — an unseeded AccessAction denies even the tenant owner while looking correct in review.
nodes.norm_label: idempotency asymmetry between create and submit

nodes.label: Legal hold enforced in the purge, not in the engine
nodes.rationale: The data_lifecycle engine only reads this delegated table, so a hold enforced inside that engine would stop nothing; purgeExpiredFormDrafts asks the injected LegalHoldGuardPort before its DELETE. Phase 1 is not gated because it deletes nothing. module.ts exports the lifecycle key and the purge imports it, so the key a hold is placed against and the key the purge checks cannot drift and fail open silently.
nodes.norm_label: legal hold enforced in the purge, not in the engine

nodes.label: evaluateAccess RBAC/ABAC decision function
nodes.rationale: Default deny, deny overrides allow, with a permission identified as module_key.activity_code.action; optional 4th and 5th parameters (businessScopeFacts, abac) keep every older call site unaffected.

nodes.label: authorizeInTransaction chokepoint
nodes.rationale: The single chokepoint every protected route calls; it resolves module enablement BEFORE looking up the permission, so a module disabled for a tenant is denied 403 MODULE_DISABLED whatever permissions the actor holds — one check that closes every endpoint of a disabled module without touching any route file. module_management is isCore so a tenant can never be locked out of re-enabling.

nodes.label: ABAC policy DSL
nodes.rationale: A restricted jsonb AST over a server-side attribute allow-list; subject attributes come from the authenticated context rather than the client body, and allow-list membership is own-property only so prototype keys cannot slip through. The parser/validator is fail-closed.

nodes.label: Pure ABAC evaluator and precedence
nodes.rationale: A pure interpreter with no eval/new Function/dynamic import/SQL. Precedence is fail-closed: an explicit satisfied deny, an invalid active policy, or any evaluation error denies BEFORE the RBAC check; allow never creates a permission and acts only as a constraint that at least one applicable policy must satisfy.

nodes.label: Tenant-keyed policy cache
nodes.rationale: Active DSL-managed policies are compiled once per tenant and invalidated deterministically after commit by every create/update/enable/disable from both surfaces; invalidation is per-process, so multi-instance would need LISTEN/NOTIFY or a TTL.

nodes.label: is_dsl_managed discriminator keeps flat policies inert
nodes.rationale: Flat #171 rows carry only effect/description/is_active and cannot be scoped or conditioned, so evaluating one deny would mean wildcard + always-true = denying EVERY request and bricking the tenant with no in-band recovery. Only the DSL surface sets is_dsl_managed true; the validator additionally rejects a deny that is unscoped and unconditional, closing the footgun on both surfaces.
nodes.norm_label: is_dsl_managed discriminator keeps flat policies inert

nodes.label: Business-scope hierarchy layer
nodes.rationale: A generic organisational authorization layer above tenant + role: scope_type/scope_id are generic references resolved through a capability port (provided by tenant_admin since ADR-0060), fail-closed for unknown or unresolved scopes, with effective dating where the row predicate is authoritative and status is only a cache, so revocation affects the very next decision without waiting for a job.

nodes.label: Composite (tenant_id, id) foreign keys
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL referential-integrity checks bypass RLS, so a single-column FK can point across tenants even with FORCE on; a composite FK carrying tenant_id closes that, proven by an integration test running as awcms_app.

nodes.label: Login audit & anti-enumeration hardening
nodes.rationale: An unknown identifier still pays for one argon2id verify against a dummy hash (removing the timing oracle) and locked answers exactly like invalid_credentials; audit attributes carry only method/reason/ipHash/userAgent, never the raw IP (redaction would empty the column) and never the login identifier (attacker-supplied PII that would itself leak enumeration). Env thresholds fall back with a warning instead of producing a NaN comparison that silently disables lockout, and X-Forwarded-For is only trusted when TRUSTED_PROXY_ENABLED is set, counted from the RIGHT because entries left of the trusted hop are attacker-writable.

nodes.label: Opaque session tokens stored as hashes
nodes.norm_label: opaque session tokens stored as hashes

nodes.label: Guards must use a seeded catalogue action
nodes.rationale: The awcms_permissions catalogue seeds identity_access.access_control with only read/assign/configure. The owner is granted every catalogue row at bootstrap, so a guard on an un-seeded action denies even the owner — which is why role/policy/user writes all guard on configure or assign rather than create/update/delete.
nodes.norm_label: guards must use a seeded catalogue action

nodes.label: Global reference rows without RLS
nodes.rationale: Province "Aceh" is the same row for every tenant, so duplicating 91,599 rows per tenant would turn reference data into storage that grows with the customer list and make "is every tenant on the same region version?" unanswerable. What replaces RLS is not trust: both tables are registered in GLOBAL_TABLE_FORBIDDEN_PRIVILEGES forcing explicit per-role privileges, neither role holds DELETE, and every endpoint still runs session → tenant context → default-deny RBAC/ABAC. What is global is the ROW, not the authorization.

nodes.label: Source provenance and the claim not made
nodes.rationale: The data is a community packaging (cahyadsn/wilayah, MIT) of the Kepmendagri decree, NOT an official Kemendagri API or export, and does not replace an operator's own legal reference. The caveat lives in exactly one place in code and is re-read by the dataset API response and the admin screen so the three cannot drift.
nodes.norm_label: source provenance and the claim not made

nodes.label: Dataset import / activate / rollback versioning
nodes.rationale: An import writes a new dataset BESIDE the previous one rather than over it, which is what makes rollback a status flip instead of a re-import; a new dataset always lands validated, never active, because importing is a deployment step while choosing what is SERVED is an audited operator decision. Only one dataset is active, enforced by a partial unique index rather than an application check two concurrent requests could interleave through.

nodes.label: Import refuses partial hierarchies
nodes.rationale: A grammar mismatch, duplicate code, orphan parent, empty tier, or checksum mismatch fails the whole import rather than importing what it could — each of those would leave regions silently missing, a self-contradicting dataset, an invisibly broken picker, a truncated file, or fictional provenance.

nodes.label: Dataset lifecycle is an operator job (ADR-0052)
nodes.rationale: Activate and rollback change the dataset served to EVERY tenant, but their permissions sat in the global catalog that setup/initialize grants wholesale to each tenant's owner — so an ordinary tenant owner held authority over data served to other tenants. These tables have no tenant_id and no RLS, so there is no tenant the action belongs to and no tenant permission can honestly express it; they became CLI operator jobs.
nodes.norm_label: dataset lifecycle is an operator job (adr-0052)

nodes.label: Ownership inversion out of news_portal (ADR-0036)
nodes.rationale: news_portal owned the registry only because the epic that needed media happened to be the news portal, leaving a brochure-site tenant with no managed media at all. The coupling lived in the port contract itself (an editorial question on the media port), so the port was SPLIT rather than renamed; table names and the reconcile command were deliberately kept because a hard composite FK and three migrations reference them.

nodes.label: Managed-media enforcement is one-way
nodes.rationale: Two halves must both hold — deployment readiness (R2 configured and separated from sync-storage credentials) and a per-tenant opt-in written by a single sanctioned entry point. There is no disable action, no unmark function and no DELETE against the state table: a tenant able to switch its own media validation off is a confirmed-exploitable path. The only rollback is a deployment-level config change, fail-closed via readiness.

nodes.label: Presigned direct-to-R2 upload flow
nodes.rationale: Finalize does a real R2 GET with magic-byte MIME sniffing and a server-side SHA-256 checksum, never a bare HEAD; R2 credentials never reach the browser, only a scoped expiring presigned URL.

nodes.label: Media object delete/restore/purge lifecycle (ADR-0056)
nodes.rationale: Three permissions sat in the catalog granted to every owner and enforced by nothing — no route, no function, no job — so an object uploaded by mistake disappeared only if the reconciliation job happened to categorise it that way. Soft delete breaks live references deliberately: a post whose featured media points at a deleted object resolves to nothing immediately.

nodes.label: Descriptor sync from the code registry
nodes.rationale: Reads the trusted in-process registry and upserts it into the database registry; naturally idempotent, and refuses to write when the registry fails dependency-graph validation.
nodes.norm_label: descriptor sync from the code registry

nodes.label: Tenant module enable/disable lifecycle
nodes.rationale: A missing tenant row means enabled by default (backward compatible), isCore modules cannot be disabled to prevent admin lockout, and disabling writes only the tenant table — it never unloads code.

nodes.label: Non-secret module settings
nodes.rationale: Tenant-aware operational preferences only: secret-shaped keys AND secret-shaped values are rejected at request time and never stored, reusing the shared redaction helpers.

nodes.label: Permission sync status report
nodes.rationale: A read-only report of synced/missing/orphaned/mismatched against the catalogue; it never writes to the catalog, which stays migration-owned.

nodes.label: Registry-derived sidebar model
nodes.rationale: The admin shell previously kept a hand-written array that had drifted into three entries pointing at non-existent pages and eight pages the registry had never heard of; the model is now derived from module declarations and bound to the filesystem in both directions by test. Navigation filtering is explicitly not authorization.

nodes.label: Module presets
nodes.rationale: A preset ENABLES what it lists and DISABLES every enabled, unlisted, unprotected module — enable-only would make presets useless as a way to reach a profile. Applied through the existing enable/disable primitives one call at a time so a rejection is reported rather than swallowed, and it guards on the stronger existing permission because a new action would need a seed migration and an unseeded action denies even the owner.

nodes.label: Tenant-module matrix
nodes.rationale: Warnings come from re-running the REAL enable/disable evaluators against each module's actual state rather than a UI-side re-derivation that can drift; it is one-directional because asking the enable evaluator about an already-enabled module short-circuits to an answer that looks like a check and is not one. No health column, because a per-row health read would be 21 queries in one transaction.

nodes.label: Sidebar arrangement stored as a delta
nodes.rationale: A tenant with no rows renders exactly the code default, which is what makes a newly added module's nav entry appear everywhere with no data migration; a snapshot would freeze each tenant's sidebar at the moment they first touched it. A tenant can override but never inject: every stored row is resolved BY KEY against the default model and unmatched rows are ignored, and overrides are applied before composition so relabelling can never carry an entry past its required permission or a disabled module.
nodes.norm_label: sidebar arrangement stored as a delta

nodes.label: maskIdentifierValue two-shape masking
nodes.rationale: An email-shaped value keeps the domain plus the first local-part letter so an admin can still tell outbox rows apart; everything else keeps only the last four characters, and nothing at all below five. The email branch is detected from the value itself rather than a type argument, because the email module masks addresses that never become a profile identifier.

nodes.label: Typed profile identifiers with value_hash
nodes.rationale: Stored as normalized_value plus a SHA-256 value_hash for dedup/resolve and a masked_value for display — never the raw value; the unique-index violation is translated and mapped to 409 INSIDE withTenant, because an error escaping outward is not a PostgresError and would count against the database circuit breaker.

nodes.label: createPersonProfileForIdentity as sole writer
nodes.rationale: Every identity-creating path used to write its own profile row and the two had already drifted — SSO JIT set verification_status verified while self-registration approval left the default, so two accounts minutes apart got different verification posture without anyone deciding it. The argument is now explicit, and false means there is no evidence of control over the address: a reviewer's say-so is not evidence, the reset link is. The function writes no audit event because the caller holds the audit over the actual decision.

nodes.label: Profile restore endpoint and its 404 symmetry
nodes.rationale: delete_reason is KEPT on restore — the deletion reason stays true and restored_at states it no longer applies. The precondition lives in the WHERE clause rather than a read-then-write, so two concurrent restores both write audit rows for one restoration. A nonexistent profile and a not-deleted profile answer with the same 404, because a distinguishable answer would turn the route into a profile-id oracle.
nodes.norm_label: profile restore endpoint and its 404 symmetry

nodes.label: Merge workflow and duplicate detection absent
nodes.norm_label: merge workflow and duplicate detection absent

nodes.label: ADR-0006 — providers are called outside the DB transaction
nodes.rationale: An external HTTP call inside a transaction holds a pool connection and a row lock for the whole round trip and turns every network failure into a rollback, re-delivering already-delivered events; no gate catches it.
nodes.norm_label: adr-0006 — providers are called outside the db transaction

nodes.label: CLAIM / SEND / FINALIZE three-phase dispatch
nodes.rationale: Two short transactions around an out-of-transaction provider call; the lease is read back so a worker that died mid-pass cannot strand a row in `sending`. Accepted trade-off: a crash between provider-accept and FINALIZE yields one duplicate notification, better than one stuck forever.

nodes.label: subscriptionGone result branch
nodes.rationale: 404/410/UNREGISTERED is a subscription reporting itself dead, not a send failure; folding it into retryable:false would leave tombstone endpoints collecting one permanent failure per message forever, so the dispatcher disables its own target.

nodes.label: An endpoint is a credential (endpoint / endpoint_hash / endpoint_masked)
nodes.rationale: Web Push endpoints and FCM tokens are bearer-ish, so they use the same three-column discipline as an email address and the raw column is named in exactly one file — the rule is holdable precisely because only one file names it.
nodes.norm_label: an endpoint is a credential (endpoint / endpoint_hash / endpoint_masked)

nodes.label: Retention delegated, not generic
nodes.rationale: HighVolumeTableDescriptor deletes purely by age with no status predicate; pointed at a queue it deletes rows still waiting to be sent and the loss looks like successful housekeeping. Every DELETE names terminal statuses and cursors on updated_at, deleting attempts -> messages -> subscriptions in FK order.

nodes.label: A dead token does not trip the circuit breaker
nodes.rationale: Only signals about the SERVICE (transport failure, 429, 5xx) trip it; counting stale tokens would let one batch of old registrations stop delivery to every healthy device with a symptom pointing at FCM. The error code is read before the status, and a 401 is refreshed exactly once.
nodes.norm_label: a dead token does not trip the circuit breaker

nodes.label: PUSH_FCM_CREDENTIALS_BASE64 + pure parser
nodes.rationale: config:validate parses .env line by line and a multi-line PEM pasted raw is silently truncated, surfacing at first send not at boot; the parser is pure and shared by validator and adapter so they cannot disagree. The RS256 assertion (RFC 7523) is signed via crypto.subtle with no dependency, and the access token is cached per process, never at rest.

nodes.label: Encryption verified against RFC 8291 vectors, not round trip
nodes.rationale: A push service does not validate the payload and a browser silently discards what it cannot decrypt, so a wrong key schedule records every send as a success and delivers nothing. A round trip only proves encryptor and decryptor agree; HKDF is built on crypto.subtle HMAC so every published intermediate (ecdh_secret, PRK_key, IKM, PRK, CEK, NONCE) is observable and reproducible.
nodes.norm_label: encryption verified against rfc 8291 vectors, not round trip

nodes.label: Ephemeral per-message ECDH key, origin-scoped VAPID aud, raw r||s ES256
nodes.rationale: One reused key pair makes every notification to a subscriber share a key schedule; signing the full endpoint instead of its origin produces a 401 that reads like a key problem. The VAPID token is cached per origin, so 500 subscribers on one push service cost one signature. Rotating the key pair does not re-key existing subscriptions.
nodes.norm_label: ephemeral per-message ecdh key, origin-scoped vapid aud, raw r||s es256

nodes.label: Service worker is not bundled by Astro
nodes.rationale: Registration is pinned to the script URL so a content-hashed name abandons every prior subscription; PUSH_SERVICE_WORKER_PATH needs a stable path; and dist/client/_astro is served immutable for a year, which a browser may keep without revalidating so a bug fix would reach nobody. Cost: it is never minified.
nodes.norm_label: service worker is not bundled by astro

nodes.label: push-target-path.ts click-target guard
nodes.rationale: A notification carrying the site's name and icon is the most convincing open-redirect vehicle; new URL(path, origin) makes protocol-relative //evil.example/x decidable where a starts-with-/ test would not. The icon is never taken from the payload, which would leak the recipient's IP and presence.

nodes.label: POST /api/v1/push/test send probe
nodes.rationale: Fixed title/body and no recipient parameter is a security boundary: a test endpoint accepting a recipient is an arbitrary-notification surface landing system-branded text on any colleague's lock screen. It exists because push fails invisibly (mismatched VAPID pair, wrong service-worker scope, OS withholding permission).

nodes.label: Self-service push subscription routes
nodes.rationale: defineSelfServiceTenantRoute (ADR-0049 §7): the subject is the caller, tenantUserId comes only from the resolved session, ownership is enforced inside the WHERE so there is no existence oracle, and revocation destroys the stored endpoint while keeping the row.

nodes.label: Latent-authz trap (inventing a permission nobody holds)
nodes.rationale: An action seeded into no role denies everyone including the owner while the calling code reads as correctly gated; push notifications are for ordinary users, so a permission wall in front of them is a wall in front of the feature.
nodes.norm_label: latent-authz trap (inventing a permission nobody holds)

nodes.label: endpoint = EXCLUDED.endpoint in the subscription upsert
nodes.rationale: The conflict target is the hash of that column so the value is usually identical; the line exists for the device re-subscribing after revocation, which would otherwise come back active while pointing at a tombstone — healthy in the console, undeliverable in reality.
nodes.norm_label: endpoint = excluded.endpoint in the subscription upsert

nodes.label: /admin/push-notifications console
nodes.rationale: Two audiences on one page on purpose: the device panel and the queue panel answer one shared question, and an operator forced across two screens would be correlating two moments in time.

nodes.label: PUSH_ENABLED feature flag behaviour when off
nodes.rationale: Without the flag dispatchPushQueue claims not a single row, making the job safe to schedule in any profile including offline/LAN; push:queue:purge runs regardless, because a deployment that turned push off still holds rows nothing else would clean up.
nodes.norm_label: push_enabled feature flag behaviour when off

nodes.label: reporting.dashboard.read (migration 010)
nodes.rationale: One permission for all five views — one dashboard feature, deliberately not split into a permission per view, including when email-health was added.

nodes.label: /admin dashboard SSR (src/pages/admin/index.astro)
nodes.rationale: Fetches the aggregations directly through withTenant rather than an HTTP round-trip to its own endpoints; missing permission renders an Access-denied panel, not an empty card and not a 500.

nodes.label: SyncIndicator (fetchSyncIndicatorActive)
nodes.rationale: A single lightweight EXISTS query rather than the full sync-health aggregation, because AdminLayout renders on every /admin/* request.

nodes.label: ProjectionDescriptor contract
nodes.rationale: Same 'module declares its own array, a central aggregator reads listModules()' shape as dataLifecycle/sodRules; the engine never writes another module's transactional table — it only reads a source and writes its own awcms_reporting_projection_* tables.

nodes.label: cursor_table update strategy
nodes.rationale: The only safe strategy for a source with no domain-event producer, but only CORRECT for a genuinely append-only source: the engine can only ADD, so a row that later disappears or is un-deleted silently desyncs the count. That is why append-only sources were wrapped and mutable/soft-delete ones (sync-health, email-health, office/profile counts) were not.

nodes.label: domain_event update strategy
nodes.rationale: Steady-state updates are pushed by a registered consumer, reusing domain_event_runtime's jobs/locks/batching/idempotency/retry machinery instead of building a second one; the one real cross-module edge is one-directional and verified cycle-free.

nodes.label: application/projection-rebuild.ts (idempotent rebuild)
nodes.rationale: triggerOrResumeRebuild is the only place cursors/metrics reset, done in the caller's own transaction atomically with the run row, audit log and idempotency record; migration 069's partial unique index makes a concurrent double-reset impossible and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING keeps a lost race from poisoning the transaction. continueRebuildPasses never resets — one bounded pass = one transaction, so a crash leaves everything consistent at the last completed pass.

nodes.label: application/event-activity-projection.ts watermark comparison
nodes.rationale: A live consumer blocked by a rebuild throws and, on retry, compares the event's occurredAt against the rebuild stream's cursor watermark; a plain skip-with-blind-retry would either permanently lose an event (rebuild cancelled before reaching it) or double-count it (rebuild completed normally). Security-auditor finding, PR #781.

nodes.label: application/projection-lock.ts (pg_advisory_xact_lock)
nodes.rationale: Per-(tenant, projection) lock taken as the first statement of every transaction writing a projection's cursor/metric rows — the mutual exclusion between rebuild and the steady-state incremental path rests on it.

nodes.label: computeProjectionFreshness (domain/freshness.ts)
nodes.rationale: A pure function of raw persisted facts vs now, never a stored status enum: if the worker stops entirely no write happens again, yet the read path still ages current -> delayed -> stale purely from elapsed time. rebuilding always wins, failed is checked after it.

nodes.label: reconcileProjection
nodes.rationale: Computes a fresh control total from the same rebuildSource and compares it to live metrics; on-demand only and no Idempotency-Key because it mutates no business state. A mismatch while merely delayed is expected — read freshness alongside reconcile, never instead of it.

nodes.label: application/export-generation.ts + scheduled exports
nodes.rationale: Deliberately minimal and self-contained rather than built on data_exchange, whose staged-import machinery fits arbitrary business-record export, not a small metric snapshot. Written outside any DB transaction, SHA-256 checksummed, CSV formula-injection neutralized, then one manifest row; download re-checks RBAC/ABAC and tenant scope and refuses an expired artifact with 410.

nodes.label: filter accepted/persisted but not applied (400 NOT_IMPLEMENTED)
nodes.rationale: Silently ignoring a submitted filter would give a false sense of scoping, so a non-empty filter is rejected until a follow-up defines its schema and wires it into generation (reviewer + security-auditor finding, PR #781).
nodes.norm_label: filter accepted/persisted but not applied (400 not_implemented)

nodes.label: domain/projection-permission-filter.ts (second enforcement layer)
nodes.rationale: The route's coarse authorizeInTransaction gate is necessary but not sufficient; each descriptor declares its own requiredPermission, filtering the list and 403ing a single-key lookup — the same pattern as filterVisibleNavigationEntries. Not yet distinguishable for today's descriptors, but it is what stops a coarse holder seeing a future narrower-permissioned projection.
